teaser.text: Carnival Corporation sells holidays that move between destinations while providing accommodation, food and entertainment aboard ship. Its business earns a dollar first by selling a place on a voyage, then by selling more of the experience around it.

stock.opening: Carnival's weighted case is $40.07 per share in October 2027 and $49.47 in October 2029. Carnival's forecast hinges on strong bookings converting into profitable sailings while Carnival funds investment and repairs its balance sheet.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Carnival's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Carnival's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: Weighted price is $40.07 in October 2027 and $44.52 in October 2028. It reaches $49.47 in October 2029. The corresponding total returns are 53% and 72% at the first two dates, then 92% at the last date.

By October 2029, the bear case reaches $25.43 while the bull case reaches $93.44, against today's $26.45. The weighting is 40% bear, 45% base and 15% bull, reflecting strong bookings but also Carnival's debt, investment needs and exposure to fuel and competition.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Carnival, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The starting point is the 2026 guide of $7,140M, just below 2025 EBITDA of $7,182M, so the forecast avoids assuming automatic expansion. The base path reflects positive yield and bookings: Q3 constant-currency net yield grew 2.4%, and roughly half of 2027 was booked at record occupancy and pricing. The bear case allows discounting, fuel pressure and faster Caribbean competition to produce an initial decline; the bull case assumes firm pricing, onboard spending and efficiency convert those bookings into faster growth.

Net debt declines in the base case because EBITDA growth exceeds cash demands, despite continued distributions. The starting proxy is $22,963M after estimated later buybacks, compared with reported August net debt of $22,692M. The bear case keeps debt near $23B through high capital spending and working-capital outflows. The bull case deleverages faster because stronger EBITDA and booking inflows outweigh larger shareholder returns. Management has also flagged $1,600M of new-ship spending and non-newbuild capital spending above $2,400M.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Carnival really make?

paragraphs.text: Net income was $2,760 million in 2025, while operating cash flow reached $6,218 million. Depreciation explains part of the difference because it lowers accounting profit without requiring another ship payment that year. Working capital can reverse the effect. In 2024, an $818 million release of credit-card reserves increased operating cash flow without increasing profit.

blocks.heading: What has Carnival guided for FY2026?

paragraphs.text: For the financial year ending November 2026, management forecasts adjusted net income of $3,080 million and diluted adjusted earnings of $2.24 per share. Adjusted profit excludes selected gains, losses and expenses, so it is an estimate of performance rather than money available to spend. Carnival must still fund its $1.08 billion interest expense, ships, debt repayment and working capital.

blocks.heading: Has Carnival kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Carnival set 2026 SEA Change targets in 2023: higher EBITDA per berth day, adjusted ROIC of 12% and lower carbon intensity. By June 2025, EBITDA per berth day had risen 52%, and adjusted ROIC was above 12.5%. Carnival also reported achieving its carbon target early. Those results support management’s credibility.

blocks.heading: How have Carnival's revenue and profit trended?
What should investors watch in Carnival's next results?

paragraphs.text: The results discussion should provide fuller 2027 assumptions for yield and capital spending. Investors should compare reported yield with the figure adjusted for Carnival Rewards, then compare higher investment with operating cash. Carnival Festivale’s planned May 2027 arrival will also test whether construction spending becomes paying capacity on schedule.

The central test is whether Carnival can make these promises advance together: higher earnings, funded ships and upgrades, lower financial strain, and shareholder returns supported by cash left after investment.
